subject: chemistry
title: Conservation of Mass
welcome_lead: Atoms do not vanish. The mass before equals the mass after, every single time.
meta_desc: Learn the conservation of mass in this KS3 chemistry adventure on chemical reactions.
final_note: You now know the most important rule in chemistry: nothing disappears.

concepts.def: Total mass of reactants equals total mass of products.
Atoms swap partners but none are made or destroyed.
Sealed container where mass cannot escape.
Mass can leave (e.g. as gas) and seem to disappear.
Amount of matter, measured in grams (g) or kg.
Equipment used to measure mass accurately.

walkthroughs.body_html:
In every chemical reaction, the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products.

Atoms cannot be created or destroyed.

walkthroughs.h2: Why does mass stay the same?
walkthroughs.body_html: The atoms simply rearrange into new combinations. If you start with 10 g of stuff, you end with 10 g of stuff — even if it looks completely different.

If a candle burns in air and gets lighter, the gas products (CO₂ and water vapour) escaped into the air. The mass looks lost but really left the container.

In a sealed jar, the mass would not change at all.

mcqs.q: What is the law of conservation of mass?
options: Atoms are destroyed in reactions
Mass of reactants equals mass of products
Mass always increases
Mass changes randomly

mcqs.q: Why does a burning candle appear to lose mass?
options: Atoms vanish
Gas products escape into the air
Wax becomes lighter
The wick weighs less

mcqs.q: If a reaction has a negative Gibbs free energy change, what does that mean?
options: A reaction with negative delta G must be exothermic in every case.
A reaction with negative delta G will always happen quickly.
The reaction is thermodynamically feasible — it can proceed — but it may still be very slow.
The oxidation state of an atom is always equal to the number of electrons it has.

mcqs.q: Why can transition metals show variable oxidation states?
options: Transition metals have variable oxidation states because they can gain protons easily.
The 4s and 3d orbitals are similar in energy, so different numbers of electrons can be removed without a large energy cost.
Transition metals have variable oxidation states because they have many shells of electrons.
The oxidation state of an atom is always equal to the number of electrons it has.

mcqs.q: Is the oxidation state of an atom the same as its actual charge?
options: A reaction with negative delta G must be exothermic in every case.
Not necessarily — oxidation state is an accounting tool assuming all bonds are fully ionic; real charge is usually smaller.
The oxidation state of an atom is exactly equal to its real ionic charge in every compound.
The oxidation state of an atom is always equal to the number of electrons it has.
